label: Col. Walter Figel Jr.
narrative: Walter Figel is the most contested witness in the American nuclear-incursion record, and he is contested in an unusual way: both sides of the Malmstrom dispute cite him, and neither has produced a statement he wrote himself. He was the deputy crew commander in the Echo Flight launch control capsule at Malmstrom AFB on the morning of 16 March 1967, sitting beside Capt. Eric D. Carlson when all ten Minuteman I missiles of the flight dropped off strategic alert at 0845. That the shutdown happened is Tier 1 and is in the 341st Strategic Missile Wing's own history. What Figel says about it is not, because it exists only as audio. Robert Hastings states he tape-recorded three telephone conversations with Figel, in 2008, 2009 and 2010, in which Figel described receiving a radio report from a topside maintenance or security man of a large round object above a launch facility as the missiles failed. James Carlson, the son of Figel's crew commander, states that Figel told him he saw no UFO and took the report as a joke. Tim Hebert, a former Malmstrom missile crew member, reads the two Hastings interviews as contradicting each other on where the maintenance teams were and on who made the report. Figel declined to sign an affidavit for the 27 September 2010 National Press Club event, which the six named affiants did sign. All three of those statements can be true at once - a man can receive a report, disbelieve it, and decline to swear to it - and the board carries them together rather than choosing. He is on the board because an informed reader would look for him and read his absence as a gap, which is exactly what CLAUDE.md section 2a now admits.
